beats.narration: Every airplane window is round. Not for looks — a seventy-year-old disaster decided that.
beats.claim: airplane windows are round by engineering necessity, not aesthetics
beats.visual_answer: a full-bleed round window holding a pressurized cabin — the shape itself is the subject

beats.narration: In 1952 the Comet was the world's first jet airliner. In 1954, two of them tore apart in clear sky — no warning.
beats.claim: the world's first commercial jet airliner broke apart twice in flight in 1954
beats.visual_question: what happens when a pressurized cabin fails at cruise?
beats.visual_answer: the Comet in flight — the era's pride — with the year of the breakups stamped on screen

beats.narration: At cruise, the cabin is pumped tight like a balloon. Pressure always finds the sharpest corner. A round opening spreads the load. A square corner gathers it.
beats.claim: cabin pressure gathers at sharp corners and spreads evenly around curves
beats.visual_question: where does the pressure load actually go?
beats.visual_answer: same pressure, two fates: square window corners glow with gathered stress, round rim stays even

beats.narration: Every flight flexes the fuselage once. In the test tank, a Comet hull burst after 3,057 flexes — against a design life of ten thousand.
beats.claim: repeated pressurization cycles grow fatigue cracks until the hull fails far short of its design life
beats.visual_question: how long until the metal fails?
beats.visual_answer: a cycle counter climbing flight by flight until 3,057 — BURST — far short of 10,000

beats.narration: The wreckage told the truth: the crack began at a square-cornered antenna window in the roof.
beats.claim: the fatal crack began at a square-cornered antenna window cutout, not the passenger windows
beats.visual_question: where exactly did the crack start?
beats.visual_answer: a fatigue crack radiating from a cutout corner in riveted skin — the origin pinned on screen

beats.narration: The fix wasn't stronger metal. It was geometry. Round everything.
beats.claim: the fix was geometry — rounding every pressurized opening
beats.visual_answer: two words as the visual: ROUND EVERYTHING

beats.narration: So when you lean on that round glass at forty thousand feet — it's round because it has to be.
beats.claim: the round window is a survival feature, inherited from 1954
beats.visual_question: what are you actually looking at?
beats.visual_answer: a round window at 40,000 ft dawn — a lesson written in wreckage, still holding
